objective: delta(n - k) picks out x(n - k), so convolving with a shifted impulse shifts and scales the signal.

subject: signals
text: The Fourier transform converts a signal from the time domain to the:

subject: signals
text: What must the sampling rate be relative to the bandwidth of a bandlimited signal to allow perfect reconstruction?
explanation: The Nyquist rate: sample strictly above twice the highest frequency so the shifted spectra do not overlap.
objective: The Nyquist rate: sample strictly above twice the highest frequency so the shifted spectra do not overlap.

subject: signals
text: The region of convergence of the z-transform of a finite-length sequence is:

explanation: Finite sums always converge except where poles at zero or infinity make the transform undefined.

subject: signals
text: Which two properties must an LTI system satisfy?
explanation: Linearity gives superposition and scaling; time invariance means a shifted input yields the same shifted output.
objective: Linearity gives superposition and scaling; time invariance means a shifted input yields the same shifted output.

subject: signals
text: An ideal low-pass filter with cutoff W passes frequencies:
explanation: Its magnitude response is 1 inside the passband |omega| <= W and 0 elsewhere.
objective: Its magnitude response is 1 inside the passband |omega| <= W and 0 elsewhere.

text: State the condition for a discrete-time LTI system to be BIBO stable in terms of its impulse response.
explanation: The impulse response must be absolutely summable: the sum of |h[n]| over all n must be finite.
objective: The impulse response must be absolutely summable: the sum of |h[n]| over all n must be finite.

subject: signals
text: Aliasing in a sampled signal is caused by:
options: Spectra replicas overlapping because the sampling rate is too low
explanation: If fs is below the Nyquist rate, the replicas centred at multiples of fs overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones.
objective: If fs is below the Nyquist rate, the replicas centred at multiples of fs overlap and high frequencies masquerade as low ones.

text: Explain the time-frequency duality implied by multiplication in one domain.
explanation: Multiplication in the time domain equals convolution in the frequency domain, and vice versa; a time shift only adds a linear phase term.
objective: Multiplication in the time domain equals convolution in the frequency domain, and vice versa; a time shift only adds a linear phase term.

text: Which of these is an even signal?

text: What is the convolution of a signal with a unit impulse?
explanation: Convolving with delta(n) returns the signal unchanged, since delta is the identity.

subject: signals
text: What does a signal's Fourier transform reveal?
explanation: It decomposes the signal into frequency components with magnitudes and phases.
objective: It decomposes the signal into frequency components with magnitudes and phases.

text: What is quantisation error?
explanation: It is the difference between the sampled amplitude and the nearest representable level, bounded by half a step.
objective: It is the difference between the sampled amplitude and the nearest representable level, bounded by half a step.

subject: signals
text: What distinguishes an FIR filter from an IIR filter?
explanation: FIR has only feed-forward terms and is always stable; IIR uses feedback so it is shorter but may be unstable.
objective: FIR has only feed-forward terms and is always stable; IIR uses feedback so it is shorter but may be unstable.

text: Why is the impulse response enough to characterise an LTI system?
explanation: Any input can be written as shifted impulses, so by superposition the output is the convolution with the impulse response.
objective: Any input can be written as shifted impulses, so by superposition the output is the convolution with the impulse response.

text: What does the unit circle in the z-plane correspond to for a digital filter?
explanation: z = e^(jw) on the unit circle, so angle maps to normalised digital frequency.
objective: z = e^(jw) on the unit circle, so angle maps to normalised digital frequency.

text: Implement a DFT brute force and print the magnitude spectrum of the given real sequence.
explanation: A brute-force DFT is O(n^2) but demonstrates exactly what the FFT computes in O(n log n).
objective: A brute-force DFT is O(n^2) but demonstrates exactly what the FFT computes in O(n log n).

subject: signals
text: Explain the Gibbs phenomenon and how it affects windowed filters.
explanation: Truncating an ideal response creates overshoot near discontinuities; smoothing windows reduce ripple at the cost of wider transitions.
objective: Truncating an ideal response creates overshoot near discontinuities; smoothing windows reduce ripple at the cost of wider transitions.

subject: signals
text: Why does AM need twice the baseband bandwidth while SSB does not?
explanation: AM transmits the carrier and both sidebands, doubling the bandwidth; single sideband transmits one sideband carrying all the information.
objective: AM transmits the carrier and both sidebands, doubling the bandwidth; single sideband transmits one sideband carrying all the information.

subject: communication
text: You need a decision from a busy colleague about a design choice. What is the most effective opening line?
options: Here is the full background on everything we have considered so far
I need a decision on X by Thursday; here are the two options and my recommendation
Are you free to chat sometime this week?
Let me know your thoughts when you get a chance
explanation: State the ask, the deadline, the options and your recommendation up front. A busy reader can decide in seconds instead of reconstructing your context.
objective: Structure a request so the reader can act immediately.

subject: communication
text: During a meeting you are unsure whether you understood a complex requirement correctly. What should you do?
options: Stay silent and implement your best guess to avoid slowing the meeting
Paraphrase the requirement in your own words and ask the speaker to confirm
Ask everyone in the room to restate the requirement
Wait until after the meeting and ask a colleague privately
explanation: Paraphrasing tests your understanding against the speaker's intent and costs only a few seconds, which prevents the most expensive class of rework.
objective: Verify understanding before acting on ambiguous requirements.

subject: communication
text: A teammate's written status update is unclear and you cannot tell what they need from you. How should you respond?
explanation: Respond with a specific clarification: restate the two possible interpretations you see, and ask which one they meant. Vague replies such as 'please clarify' push the work back without reducing ambiguity.
objective: Resolve ambiguity efficiently without adding friction.

subject: communication
text: Explain why leading with the conclusion is usually more effective than building up to it, and describe one situation where a bottom-up structure is genuinely better.
explanation: Leading with the conclusion respects the listener's time and lets them stop reading once they agree, which suits decision-makers. Bottom-up is better when the audience is skeptical or needs to follow the reasoning to trust the claim, such as a contested technical proposal or a legal argument.
objective: Choose a communication structure based on audience and purpose.

subject: teamwork
text: You are handing your unfinished work to a teammate while you are on leave. What makes the best handover?
options: A link to the code repository and nothing else
The goal, current state, the next step, and any known risks or open questions
A complete verbal walkthrough recorded as a video
A promise to answer questions from holiday
explanation: A handover should let the next person work without you. Goal, state, next step and known risks give them everything needed to continue and to decide.
objective: Hand over work so a teammate can continue without you.

subject: teamwork
text: In a fully remote team, which behaviour most reduces coordination friction?
options: Answering all questions as fast as possible, even with incomplete information
Posting status, decisions and blockers in a place the whole team can find them
Keeping work private until it is finished to avoid noisy updates
Scheduling a meeting for every question to keep discussion synchronous
explanation: Remote teams cannot rely on overhearing context. Writing state, decisions and blockers where everyone can find them is what replaces the shared room.
objective: Make collaboration state visible in distributed teams.

subject: teamwork
text: A teammate's approach seems wrong to you, and you disagree strongly. How should you raise it in a team discussion?
explanation: Critique the artifact rather than the author: name the weakest assumption or the evidence that concerns you, and state what would change your mind. This keeps the disagreement technical and keeps the person on your side of the table.
objective: Disagree without damaging the working relationship.

subject: teamwork
text: A team repeatedly misses its weekly commitment. Explain how you would diagnose whether the cause is individual skill, coordination overhead, or unclear ownership, and what you would change first.
explanation: Separate the causes with evidence: rework and long cycle times point to skill or unclear acceptance criteria, waiting and handoff delays point to coordination, and unfinished work with no named owner points to ownership. Change the smallest thing that removes the observed bottleneck first, then measure again before adding process.
objective: Diagnose team failure modes with evidence before adding process.

subject: leadership
text: You notice a recurring problem that nobody owns. What is the best first step as someone without formal authority?
options: Wait for a manager to assign it to someone
Take the cheap, reversible part of it and show a small result
Write a detailed proposal and send it to leadership
Raise it in a meeting so everyone is aware of it
explanation: Initiative without authority works by starting small and reversible. A visible result earns the standing to propose the larger change later.
objective: Exercise initiative proportionate to risk and authority.

subject: leadership
text: You are blocked on an external dependency and the delay will affect a deadline. What is the most professional response?
options: Keep working around it quietly and hope it resolves before the deadline
State the blocker, the impact, the options, and your recommendation, then ask for a decision
Escalate immediately to your manager without context
Silently absorb the delay and report it at the deadline
explanation: Escalating with impact, options and a recommendation turns a hidden risk into a fast decision. Escalating with no context just moves the work.
objective: Escalate blockers with impact and a recommendation.

subject: leadership
text: You are delegating a task you could do faster yourself. What should you hand over, and what should you hold back?
explanation: Hand over the goal, the constraints and the definition of done, and stay available for questions. Hold back only the decisions that are genuinely yours. Dictating the steps keeps you the bottleneck and teaches nothing.
objective: Delegate outcomes while retaining appropriate control.

subject: leadership
text: Your team wants to adopt a new tool that you believe will slow delivery. You have no authority to block it. How do you influence the decision responsibly?
explanation: Influence by converting your objection into evidence and a cheap test: propose the criteria that would prove the tool helps, a time-boxed pilot on a small piece of work, and the measurement that would settle it. If the pilot shows you were wrong, you have learned something; if it confirms your concern, the decision has data behind it. Blocking or sulking are both weak.
objective: Influence technical decisions with evidence when lacking authority.

subject: time_management
text: Your day is full of urgent but low-value requests. Which approach protects the work that actually matters?
options: Work through them in arrival order to avoid missing anything
Block time first for the one or two tasks that define a good day, then batch the rest
Extend your working hours to fit everything
Ask your manager to prioritise every request for you
explanation: Urgency is a property of the clock, importance of the outcome. Protecting a block for high-consequence work first is what stops a busy day from becoming an empty one.
objective: Prioritise by consequence rather than urgency.

subject: time_management
text: Why does a single notification during deep work cost more than the minute it takes to read?
options: It does not; one minute is one minute
It forces a context reload, so the lost time is much larger than the interruption itself
Notifications consume network bandwidth that slows your machine
It only costs time if you act on the notification
explanation: Attention has to be rebuilt after each switch. The interruption itself is small; the reload of context and the fragmentation of the block are the real cost.
objective: Understand the true cost of interruption.

subject: time_management
text: You consistently overcommit and finish the week behind. Describe a concrete weekly habit that would fix the root cause rather than the symptom.
explanation: Work to a weekly capacity rather than a task list: count the realistic hours available, subtract fixed meetings and support load, and commit to what fits with buffer for the unexpected. The habit is reviewing the committed list at the start of each week and naming explicitly what will be dropped when new work arrives.
objective: Manage commitment capacity rather than reacting to overload.

subject: time_management
text: Three important tasks must finish this week and only one can realistically be done well. Explain how you decide which to drop, and how you communicate it.
explanation: Rank by consequence and dependency: what breaks for whom if this slips, and what cannot be recovered later. Drop the item whose delay is recoverable, then tell the affected stakeholders explicitly which item moved, why, and when it will land. Silent partial delivery on all three is the worst outcome because it destroys trust in every estimate.
objective: Make explicit trade-offs under genuine time constraints.

subject: adaptability
text: A requirement you spent two weeks implementing is cancelled. What is the most useful immediate response?
options: Continue polishing it in case the requirement returns
Ask what changed, salvage the reusable parts, and record the assumption that failed
Move on silently and delete the work
Push to reinstate the requirement since the effort was already spent
explanation: Sunk effort should not drive the next decision. Understanding what changed, keeping what is reusable, and recording the failed assumption is what makes the loss productive.
objective: Respond constructively to invalidated work.

subject: adaptability
text: You receive harsh feedback that feels unfair. What is the most productive first move?
options: Explain why the feedback is wrong in detail
Ask for the specific observation behind the judgement, then evaluate it on its merits
Accept it completely to avoid conflict
Ignore it because the reviewer lacks context
explanation: General judgements hide specific observations. Asking for the observation separates the useful signal from the tone, and lets you judge each on its merits rather than accepting or rejecting the whole.
objective: Extract signal from critical feedback.

subject: adaptability
text: A framework you have used for years is being replaced by a different approach in your team. How do you adapt without discarding what you already know?
explanation: Deliberately identify which of your old defaults the new approach breaks, and which still apply. Map the concepts across so you keep the transferable knowledge, and consciously retire the habits that now mislead. Unlearning is part of learning, not a loss.
objective: Adapt existing expertise to a new approach.

subject: adaptability
text: You must make an important decision with incomplete information and no way to get certainty in time. Explain how you decide and how you protect against being wrong.
explanation: Decide on the best available evidence, list the assumptions the decision rests on, and prefer the option that is cheap to reverse. Define in advance what signal would prove the decision wrong and when you will check for it, plus a fallback if it appears. Certainty is not available; a plan for being wrong is.
objective: Decide under uncertainty with explicit safeguards.

subject: conflict_resolution
text: Two colleagues hold opposite positions on a design. What question best moves the conversation forward?
options: Who has more experience with this kind of system?
What outcome is each of you trying to protect, and what constraints do both of you have to respect?
Which option is cheaper to implement right now?
Can we table this and move on?
explanation: Positions hide interests. Asking what each side is protecting usually reveals a shared constraint, which opens options neither side had proposed.
objective: Move from positions to interests in a disagreement.

subject: conflict_resolution
text: A disagreement is becoming personal in a meeting. What should you do first?
options: State your position more forcefully so the meeting can conclude
Acknowledge what is true in their position and move the discussion to shared facts
Ask a senior person to decide immediately
End the meeting and let everyone cool off without any follow-up
explanation: Nobody accepts a proposal from someone they feel unheard by. Lowering the temperature by acknowledging what is valid, then focusing on agreed facts, is what makes resolution possible.
objective: De-escalate before persuading.

subject: conflict_resolution
text: A technical disagreement was resolved, but the discussion left tension between you and a colleague. What should you do, and why?
explanation: Repair the relationship explicitly: a short private follow-up acknowledging the friction and confirming you value the working relationship. Resolved disagreements still leave residue, and unaddressed residue quietly degrades every later decision.
objective: Repair relationships after conflict.

subject: conflict_resolution
text: A stakeholder insists on an approach you believe is technically unsound, and they will not accept your reasoning. Describe how you proceed without damaging the relationship.
explanation: Find the interest behind their insistence, often a deadline, a customer promise or a past failure. Convert your objection into shared criteria and a cheap reversible test that would settle it, and document the risks and the agreed decision rule. If they still insist, record the concern and the decision owner, and plan the mitigation rather than fighting to the last.
objective: Handle persistent disagreement while protecting the relationship and the outcome.

subject: emotional_intelligence
text: You notice your written replies getting shorter and sharper as a review becomes tense. What is the best immediate action?
options: Send one more comment to make the technical point final
Pause, note that you are activated, and decide deliberately whether to reply now
Reply later at night when you have thought about it more
Ask the other person why they are being difficult
explanation: Noticing your own state is the first skill; naming it without judgement reduces its grip and creates a deliberate pause before you act on it.
objective: Recognise and regulate your own emotional state.

subject: emotional_intelligence
text: A colleague reacts strongly to a change you consider minor. What does acting with empathy mean here?
options: Agreeing that the change is a bad idea
Forming a hypothesis about their concern, checking it, and accounting for it in how you proceed
Explaining calmly that the reaction is disproportionate
Leaving them out of the conversation to reduce friction
explanation: Empathy is a checked hypothesis, not mind reading and not agreement. Understanding the concern lets you address the actual risk rather than the stated objection.
objective: Practise empathy as hypothesis and response.

subject: emotional_intelligence
text: You are too stressed to make a good decision on a request in front of you. What is the professional way to handle it?
explanation: Say your state plainly and buy time: that you want to give the request proper attention and will respond by a specific time. Announcing your state is allowed and usually respected, and a committed later response is far better than a pressured wrong answer now.
objective: Regulate state under pressure professionally.

subject: emotional_intelligence
text: A team member's performance has dropped and you suspect a personal problem. Explain how you respond as their colleague without overstepping.
explanation: Approach privately, describe the change in work terms you have observed, and offer practical support such as adjusted deadlines or a lighter load. Do not diagnose or pry: the private matter is theirs to share. Keep what they tell you confidential and point to the proper support channels. Care is expressed through concrete relief, not curiosity.
objective: Support a struggling colleague with appropriate boundaries.

subject: workplace_ethics
text: A metric you are reporting came out worse than expected. What is the professional action?
options: Report the number as measured and explain what it means
Adjust the methodology until the number looks reasonable
Leave it out of the report this cycle
Report it verbally and skip the written record
explanation: Integrity is reporting what you measured, especially when it is inconvenient. Changing the method to fit the desired answer is the classic small compromise that erodes trust.
objective: Report results honestly under pressure.

subject: workplace_ethics
text: A colleague confides in you about a private matter concerning a third colleague. What is the right handling?
options: Share it with the team so everyone has context
Keep it confidential and do not repeat it, including to close colleagues
Use it to decide whether to trust them professionally
Tell the third colleague so the situation can be resolved openly
explanation: Confidentiality is part of the job, and it holds even when the information is no longer interesting. Repeating private information damages trust permanently.
objective: Handle confidential information responsibly.

subject: workplace_ethics
text: You believe a shortcut being taken to hit a release date creates a real risk to users. Describe the right way to raise it.
explanation: Raise it early, in writing, through the defined channel, describing the observed risk rather than your conclusions. Make sure the decision is visible and owned by someone accountable, and record your concern. Early documented reporting is treated as diligence; silence later looks like complicity.
objective: Escalate risk concerns responsibly.

subject: workplace_ethics
text: You are asked to take credit in a presentation for work a junior colleague did most of. You are also under pressure to look strong. Explain how you handle it and why.
explanation: Name the colleague's contribution specifically and publicly. Credit compounds trust and is the cheapest reputation you will ever build, while taking undeserved credit is the single most visible way to lose it. If the pressure is about visibility, describe your own contribution honestly rather than borrowing theirs.
objective: Handle credit and visibility ethically.

subject: career_planning
text: Which habit best supports deliberate career growth?
options: Applying to every interesting job posting you see
Naming the role you want next, identifying the gap, and collecting evidence that closes it
Collecting as many certifications as possible
Waiting until you feel ready before changing anything
explanation: Growth compounds from a chosen direction and collected evidence. Certifications and applications are outputs; a named target and closed gap are what actually move a career.
objective: Direct career growth deliberately.

subject: career_planning
text: When is the strongest professional network usually built?
options: Continuously, by being useful to people before you need anything from them
At large conferences once a year
By connecting with as many senior people as possible
explanation: Networks are built through small, unsolicited usefulness over time. The value shows up later, when someone already knows your work and can vouch for it.
objective: Build a professional network as maintenance.

subject: career_planning
text: You are asked a technical question you do not know the answer to. How should you respond in an interview?
explanation: Clarify the question, then think aloud: state what you do know, how you would approach it, what the trade-offs would be, and how you would find the answer. Interviewers are sampling how you think under uncertainty; a transparent reasoning process scores better than a bluffed answer.
objective: Handle unknown questions by demonstrating reasoning.

subject: career_planning
text: You want to move into a role you have no direct experience in. Explain how you build a credible case for the transition.
explanation: Close the gap with adjacent work and visible outcomes: take the internal project that resembles the target role, produce a measurable result, and write it up. Find someone already in the role to review your plan and tell you what they would look for. The credible case is a body of evidence plus a named gap and a plan, not a statement of interest.
objective: Build evidence for a role transition.

subject: presentation
text: What is the strongest opening for a technical talk to a mixed audience?
options: An agenda slide listing every topic you will cover
The situation, the problem or opportunity, and what the audience will get
explanation: Opening with situation, problem and payoff tells the audience why to listen and gives them a thread to hold. Agendas and credentials spend the most valuable attention on the least valuable content.
objective: Open a presentation with a clear frame.

subject: presentation
text: Nerves before a talk are best handled by which preparation?
options: Memorising the entire talk word for word
Knowing your first two sentences and your closing cold, and rehearsing the transitions
Adding more detail to the slides so you can read them
Avoiding rehearsal so the talk feels spontaneous
explanation: Nerves mostly vanish once you are speaking, so the risk is the opening and the hand-offs. Knowing those cold, plus the landing, removes the places where talks actually break.
objective: Prepare delivery to manage nerves.

subject: presentation
text: You are given a dense slide full of bullet points for an important review. What do you do with it?
explanation: Split it: one idea per slide with a single takeaway, and move the detail into an appendix or a written handout for those who need it. A slide that is read aloud teaches nothing; a slide that makes one clear claim supports the argument.
objective: Design slides that support comprehension.

subject: presentation
text: You must present a project that failed partway through its goal. Explain how you structure that talk so the audience trusts your judgement.
explanation: Open with the goal and the outcome, then the evidence of what actually happened rather than a narrative of who did what. Separate what is now known from what was assumed, state the cost of the failure honestly, and end with a concrete recommendation. Audiences trust candour with a forward decision far more than a spin or a defensive account.
objective: Present failure credibly and usefully.
